problems.desc: Part (b) rubric: a correct response names the figure an isosceles trapezoid, and justifies it from the two stated properties --- exactly one pair of parallel sides makes it a trapezoid, and the two pairs of equal base angles (108 degrees with 108 degrees and 72 degrees with 72 degrees) make that trapezoid isosceles. Naming trapezoid alone, without the isosceles refinement or without citing the angle pairs, earns partial credit.

Part (b) rubric: a correct response names the figure a parallelogram and says why the given property is enough: a quadrilateral whose diagonals bisect each other is a parallelogram, which is exactly what equal segments on either side of the intersection mean. A response must also acknowledge that nothing given rules the figure in or out as a rectangle, rhombus or square, so parallelogram is the most specific name available.

Part (b) rubric: a correct response names the figure a square and builds it from both given properties --- four congruent sides make it a rhombus, and congruent diagonals force the angles to be right angles, so the rhombus is also a rectangle, and a figure that is both is a square. Naming square without connecting each property to the step it supplies earns partial credit.

Part (c) rubric: a correct response names the figure a parallelogram, because both pairs of opposite angles being congruent is one of the standard tests for a parallelogram, and then states that the figure would additionally be a rectangle if the angles were all equal, that is all 90 degrees --- equivalently if one angle were a right angle, or if the diagonals were congruent. Full credit requires both the classification and a workable extra condition.

Part (a) rubric: a rhombus is only sometimes a square. A correct response says a rhombus has four congruent sides but its angles need not be right angles, gives or describes a non-square rhombus as the case that fails, and notes that a rhombus with right angles is a square, so both outcomes occur.

Part (b) rubric: a square is always a rhombus. A correct response says a square has four congruent sides, which is the defining property of a rhombus, so every square satisfies it; the extra right angles a square carries do not stop it from qualifying.

Part (c) rubric: a trapezoid, defined here as having exactly one pair of parallel sides, is never a parallelogram. A correct response says a parallelogram needs both pairs of opposite sides parallel while the trapezoid is stated to have exactly one, so the two conditions cannot hold together. A response that notes the inclusive definition of trapezoid and reasons correctly from it may be accepted, provided it states which definition it is using.

Part (a) rubric: a correct response names the figure a rectangle. Diagonals that bisect each other make it a parallelogram, and congruent diagonals make that parallelogram a rectangle; because the diagonals are stated not to be perpendicular, it is not a square, so rectangle is the most specific name.

Part (c) rubric: a correct response says a square's diagonals are perpendicular, and this figure's diagonals are stated not to be, so the figure fails a property every square has. Citing instead that a square's diagonals bisect the angles of the figure, or that all four sides would then be congruent, is acceptable provided the response ties the failure to a property squares must have.

Part (b) rubric: a correct response names the figure a kite and explains that its congruent sides are adjacent in two pairs rather than opposite, so the two pairs have different lengths (17 centimetres and 14 centimetres). A rhombus would need all four sides congruent, which fails here, and that contrast must appear for full credit.

Part (a) rubric: a correct response gives a kite as the counterexample and describes the arrangement --- its two pairs of congruent sides are adjacent, sharing a vertex, rather than opposite each other, so no pair of opposite sides need be parallel or congruent. Any correct counterexample with an accurate description of how its congruent sides sit is acceptable; simply naming a shape is not.
